prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, establishing moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery with a clean origin and a clean split between theory and experiment. Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands at a specific twist angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group showed that the predicted regime hosts correlated insulators and superconductivity. That created a whole platform, moire materials, in which stacking and interface geometry become a design parameter for electronic phases. Five of the seven members who ranked it put it in the top three or five, and it was named by Danielsson, Lindroth, Mehlig and Pearce as a clear prediction-plus-confirmation story, so it has broad support rather than a single advocate. Eight years of reproduction by independent groups mean the observations are stable. Treating the prize as one for a discovery rather than lifetime achievement, as I have said the criteria require, the identifiable discovery here is the flat-band prediction and the 2018 experiments, and the three credited names map onto it directly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated, twist-angle inhomogeneity makes sample dependence a real issue, and Lindroth is right that recognition may be somewhat early for the superconducting part even if the flat-band and moire concept is secure. The three-name limit also leaves out first authors and other experimental groups (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Kim, Yazdani, Efetov), so any citation will look contestable. By contrast, optical lattice clocks (B041) have a two-name allocation that nearly every member found clean, the technology is fully mature, and it drew six top-three rankings. I cannot honestly claim B017 is a safer prize than B041, only that I judge its scientific novelty and field-creating effect to be larger.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as the cleanest case: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal plus Ye's record stability, mature, independently reproduced worldwide, and a clear route to redefining the second, with a two-laureate configuration.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and maturity assessment and I rank B041 second for those reasons; it is the most defensible alternative on this list. Where I differ is on weighting. Clocks are a superb refinement of a lineage the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) already recognised, whereas twisted bilayer graphene opened a new class of correlated matter. I also note the point you yourself make about Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow and Hinkley: the clean two-person story still omits real contributors. If the committee values a safe, uncontested allocation above field-creating novelty, B041 is the right choice and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first, as the opening of neutrino astronomy and an answer to where cosmic rays are accelerated, with Halzen as the driving force and Karle central, but concedes that allocation among a collaboration of several hundred is the real difficulty and that the TXS association rests on modest significance.
responses.response: The science is a genuine discovery and I ranked it fifth, but I do not think it fits the prize as well as you do. Your own attribution caveat is decisive for me: if Yoshida is not clearly decisive and the credit is spread across a collaboration of hundreds, then the instrument is more securely credited than the discovery. Source identification at the TXS and NGC 1068 level is still maturing, as Mehlig also notes. By comparison, twisted graphene has a sharp prediction and a sharp experiment with named originators. I would reconsider if you can show that Halzen and Karle alone carry the diffuse-flux discovery, but that has not been argued from the ballots.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks altermagnetism first as a third class of collinear magnetic order from spin-group symmetry and first-principles theory, with ARPES confirmations in MnTe and CrSb, but acknowledges priority questions from earlier symmetry-based work and that device relevance is not demonstrated.
responses.response: I take altermagnetism seriously and the symmetry classification is a real conceptual advance, but it is not on my list and I think it is early. The experimental evidence is a handful of materials and the anomalous-Hall signals are still being sorted out, and you note yourself that priority disputes with Hayami, Yanagi, Kusunose and Yuan and Zunger exist. Twisted graphene is no less young, but its core observations have been reproduced across many groups for eight years. I would be happy to revisit altermagnetism in a later cycle once the priority question and the materials base are firmer.

responses.point: Johansson ranks topological insulators first (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, with Hasan in his configuration), calling it a textbook prediction-confirmation sequence that reshaped condensed matter, and notes that leaving out Mele is a real cost of the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree that this is a major discovery and that the maturity is excellent, so on science alone it is a strong rival to B017. My reservation is the one you and Eriksson both raise: the credit set is genuinely broken by the three-name limit, because Kane-Mele is a joint contribution, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not among the credited names, and Hasan's 3D work is a separate discovery. The 2016 prize on topological phases also overlaps in subject. I would put this just behind twisted graphene because the B017 split between prediction and experiment is easier to state in a citation without choosing between co-authors of one paper.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems first as exact, general, extensively tested statements about work and entropy production far from equilibrium, while noting that credit among Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert has to be split and some foundational contributors are outside the credited set.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual content, and your point that the results are now tested in many experiments is fair. My difficulty is that it is a framework with several independent originators over a decade, so the answer to who is responsible for the original work is less sharp than the committee asks for; your own allocation sentence lists four different contributions. I also note that only you ranked it, so it does not currently have the cross-committee support that the other leading candidates do. I would want to see an argument for a unique citation before moving it up.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers the clearest two-person allocation (B041) over the more field-creating but more contested-attribution B017.
Whether the superconductivity mechanism and twist-angle inhomogeneity make B017 premature for 2026, in line with Lindroth's maturity concern.
Whether the three credited names in B017 are the best allocation given the contributions of Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Kim and others.
Whether a second closely related condensed-matter or spintronics topic (B008, B004) would be preferred given the 2007 and 2016 prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. My connections are general: Chalmers colleagues in microscopy and materials physics, including committee member Goran Johansson, who ranks circuit QED (B028) and topological insulators (B004), and academic exchanges in Japan, which is relevant only in the sense that Katori and Miyazaki work there; I have no documented relationship with any credited person and would flag a recusal if one emerged.
